scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire study is a multicenter Japanese cohort of COVID-19 patients followed for 36 months to characterize 'long COVID' symptom trajectories and clusters; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the document.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a Japanese multicenter retrospective cohort study that followed 515 adults hospitalized with COVID-19 (first to third pandemic waves, Jan 2020-Feb 2021) for 36 months using questionnaires. It grouped patients both by symptom trajectory (continuous, relapsed, recovered, late-onset, never) and by symptom-cluster patterns measured at 3 months, then tracked quality of life (SF-36) and self-reported work-productivity (WHO Health and Work Performance Questionnaire presenteeism/absenteeism scores) and subjective economic condition through 36 months. It found that a substantial minority of patients still had persistent or relapsing symptoms (fatigue and dyspnea especially) at 3 years, that patients in the 'multiple symptoms' cluster and the 'continuous' trajectory group had the worst quality-of-life and work-productivity scores, and that a higher proportion of patients with more symptoms or continuous symptoms reported their economic situation had worsened. No dollar costs are reported anywhere in the study; burden is measured only through self-reported scales and percentages within this specific Japanese hospitalized cohort.

contextual_issues: Direct medical costs (clinic visits, tests, medications, hospitalizations) for long COVID are not measured or reported anywhere in this document.
Direct non-medical costs such as travel for care or paid caregiving help are not measured or reported.
Actual monetary lost income or wages is not reported; only unitless WHO HPQ presenteeism/absenteeism scores and categorical self-reported 'economic condition' changes are captured.
Caregiver time or caregiver strain is not measured, though the paper's framing of 'economic conditions' implies household-level effects it does not quantify.
Insurance coverage, access barriers, or out-of-pocket burden are not discussed.

Diagnostic delay to initial COVID-19 diagnosis or long COVID recognition is not analyzed as a burden category; the focus is on symptom persistence after an already-confirmed PCR/antigen-positive diagnosis.
Anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale) and vaccination status were collected but specific quantified mental-health burden results are not reported in the sections provided.
evidence_gaps: No monetized direct medical or non-medical cost data are reported for this cohort; converting presenteeism/absenteeism scores or 'economic condition worsened' percentages into dollar or yen figures would require an external wage/cost model not provided in this document.
No long-term financial outcome data (debt, benefit claims, job loss counts) are reported beyond the subjective 5-point 'economic condition' question.

The study lacks objective clinical/biomarker confirmation of long COVID (no blood tests or imaging), which the authors themselves note limits the ability to separate long COVID from reinfection-driven symptom recurrence.

No healthy-control comparison group was included, so the authors state it is unclear whether changes in economic condition were due to long COVID specifically or to pandemic-era life circumstances generally.
comparison_boundaries: This is a Japanese hospitalized-cohort study (waves 1-3, Jan 2020-Feb 2021); its symptom-persistence and productivity-score findings should not be pooled with U.S. general-population Long COVID prevalence estimates (e.g., CDC survey data), which use different populations, case definitions, and non-hospitalized community samples.

The 12-month finding of a female-vs-male odds ratio of 2.54 (from the authors' earlier publication on the same base cohort) and the 36-month finding of no sex difference are measurements at different follow-up time windows using what may be different subsets/completers of the cohort; they describe change over time, not a single stable sex effect, and must not be merged into one number.

The 'symptom trajectory' classification (continuous/relapse/recovered/late-onset/never, based on presence over the full 36 months) and the 'symptom cluster' classification (based on a one-time cluster analysis of 24 symptoms at 3 months) are two different analytic schemes applied to the same 515 patients; cluster membership and trajectory group are related but not identical categories and should not be treated as interchangeable inputs.

WHO HPQ presenteeism and absenteeism are self-reported productivity-impairment scores, not monetized lost-wage estimates; they cannot be converted to a dollar cost without an assumed wage rate that this document does not supply.

The document's own comparison to Chinese 36-month cohort studies (Han et al.; Zhang et al.) involved populations with a much higher proportion requiring oxygen supplementation (74.3% vs. 34.4% in this study), so symptom-prevalence rates across these studies reflect different severity mixes and should not be pooled into a single rate.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The authors' prior analysis of the same base cohort found a higher risk of long COVID among females than males at 12 months (odds ratio 2.54, 95% CI 1.43-4.53). In the current 36-month analysis, no significant difference in the proportion with vs. without long COVID was observed by sex (Table 1: male 66.7% in long-COVID group vs. 60.1% in non-long-COVID group, p=0.18), which the authors suggest indicates the impact of sex on long COVID decreased by 3 years.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The presenteeism/absenteeism scores and the 'economic condition worsened' percentages (by symptom trajectory group, by symptom cluster, and by symptom count) are reported pooled across the cohort without further breakdown by sex, age group, or any other demographic subgroup, even though sex and age were collected in Table 1; the document does not state that subgroup variation in these economic/productivity outcomes was checked and found negligible.

scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a Japanese multicenter retrospective cohort study that followed 515 adults hospitalized with COVID-19 (first to third pandemic waves, Jan 2020-Feb 2021) for 36 months using questionnaires. It grouped patients both by symptom trajectory (continuous, relapsed, recovered, late-onset, never) and by symptom-cluster patterns measured at 3 months, then tracked quality of life (SF-36) and self-reported work-productivity (WHO Health and Work Performance Questionnaire presenteeism/absenteeism scores) and subjective economic condition through 36 months. spec.title: Long COVID Symptom Patterns and Self-Reported Work/Economic Impact (Japanese 36-Month Cohort)
spec.boundary: This simulator reflects only a 515-adult Japanese multicenter cohort of patients hospitalized for COVID-19 (pandemic waves 1-3, January 2020-February 2021), followed by self-report questionnaire to 36 months (survey conducted November 2023-February 2024). It covers self-reported work-performance impairment scores (WHO Health and Work Performance Questionnaire presenteeism/absenteeism) and self-reported 'economic condition worsened' percentages by symptom trajectory group or symptom-count subgroup. It does not include any direct medical costs, non-medical costs, caregiver costs, or monetized lost wages - none of these are reported anywhere in the document. Findings are specific to this hospitalized Japanese cohort and should not be generalized to non-hospitalized populations or other countries.

takeaway.patient: In this Japanese study of 515 adults hospitalized with COVID-19 and followed for three years, people whose long COVID symptoms continued the whole time, or who had several symptoms at once, were more likely to report that their work performance was affected and that their overall economic situation had gotten worse, compared with people whose symptoms went away. For example, about 44% of the continuous-symptom group reported their economic situation worsened, versus about 15% of those who recovered - a gap of roughly 29 percentage points, which the study found statistically significant. These are self-reported scores and percentages from one cohort, not dollar costs, and they describe what the study found in this group, not what will happen to any individual person.
takeaway.care: Among the 515 adults hospitalized with COVID-19 in this Japanese cohort followed to 36 months, patients in the 'continuous' symptom trajectory or the 'multiple symptoms' cluster (identified at 3 months) had the worst self-reported work-performance (presenteeism) scores and the highest rates of self-reported economic worsening (about 44% in the continuous group vs about 15% in the recovered group, a roughly 29-percentage-point gap, p<0.001 across trajectory groups). A similar pattern appeared between patients with five-or-more versus one-to-four symptoms (about 47% vs 24%), though the document does not report a significance test for that specific comparison. These patterns may help identify which post-COVID patients could benefit from earlier vocational or rehabilitation referral, though the study provides no cost or wage data to size that need financially.
takeaway.policy: In this 515-patient Japanese multicenter cohort of adults hospitalized with COVID-19 (waves 1-3, January 2020-February 2021) followed to 36 months, 25.6% (132/515) met the study's long COVID definition at 3 years. Among symptomatic patients, those with a continuous symptom trajectory reported substantially higher rates of self-reported economic worsening (43.6%) than those who recovered (14.9%), a roughly 29-percentage-point gap found statistically significant (p<0.001); a similar, non-significance-tested gap (about 23 percentage points) was observed between patients with five-or-more versus one-to-four symptoms. No direct medical costs, non-medical costs, or monetized productivity losses are reported anywhere in this study - only unitless WHO HPQ presenteeism/absenteeism scores and categorical self-report items from this one hospitalized Japanese cohort.

patient: If experiencing several ongoing long COVID symptoms together, consider raising with a clinician whether exploring work-accommodation or rehabilitation support earlier might be worthwhile, since the study linked having multiple ongoing symptoms with worse self-rated work performance.

When comparing personal experience to this study, keep in mind it followed hospitalized adults in Japan for three years using questionnaires, not a direct measure of costs, and it reported group patterns, not a prediction for any one person.

If a 'presenteeism' or 'absenteeism' score comes up in care discussions, ask what it means in plain terms - it is a self-rated measure of how much symptoms got in the way of work performance, not a diagnosis or a cost figure.
care: Consider whether the 3-month symptom-cluster classification, especially a 'multiple symptoms' pattern, could be worth checking against local follow-up protocols as an early flag for patients who may benefit from earlier occupational-health or rehabilitation referral.

Review whether longer-term follow-up scheduling distinguishes between continuous, relapsing, and recovered symptom trajectories, since these groups diverged sharply in self-reported productivity and economic outcomes in this cohort.

Note that the absenteeism-score comparison between long-COVID and non-long-COVID patients did not reach statistical significance (p=0.94) in this cohort, unlike the presenteeism-score comparison (p=0.003) - avoid treating these two work-impact measures as equally well-supported when designing outreach criteria.

Consider adding a routine self-reported economic-condition follow-up item for long COVID patients, mirroring this study's approach, since no monetized cost data exists in this document to substitute for it.
policy: Treat the trajectory-group and symptom-count patterns as a qualitative, non-monetized signal of which post-COVID patient profiles may warrant longer-term disability or return-to-work policy attention, recognizing this document provides no cost basis for sizing that need.

Consider this study's self-reported economic-worsening percentages (continuous vs recovered groups) as one input worth weighing in disability/accommodation policy discussions, understanding they are subjective single-item self-reports from a hospitalized Japanese cohort, not validated income-loss measures.

Avoid pooling this cohort's 36-month prevalence (25.6%) or productivity-score findings with non-hospitalized or non-Japanese Long COVID surveillance estimates, since they use different populations, case definitions, and settings.

If pursuing cost-effectiveness or burden estimates for long COVID policy, note that this document supplies no dollar or yen figure and would require an external wage/cost model plus a separate monetization methodology not provided here.

package.documentation:
This simulator is built from a Japanese multicenter retrospective cohort study of 515 adults hospitalized for COVID-19 (pandemic waves 1-3, January 2020-February 2021), followed by questionnaire to 36 months (survey conducted November 2023-February 2024). The document reports no direct medical costs, non-medical costs, caregiver costs, or monetized lost wages anywhere; all burden measures here are self-reported percentages or WHO Health and Work Performance Questionnaire (HPQ) presenteeism/absenteeism scores, which rate self-perceived work performance and are not dollar figures.

Inputs: the percentage of the continuous-symptom-trajectory group and the recovered-trajectory group who reported their economic condition had worsened by 36 months (Fig. 5a, p.7); the same comparison by symptom count (five-or-more vs one-to-four symptoms, p.6); the presenteeism score for the continuous-trajectory group (Fig. 5b, p.8) and for the 'multiple symptoms' cluster identified at 3 months (Table 2, p.5). Exploration ranges for the two trajectory-group percentages were narrowed deliberately so sliders cannot reverse the ordering the study found statistically significant (p<0.001): the continuous group's share stays above the recovered group's share across the chosen ranges. The symptom-count comparison and the presenteeism scores use wider, illustrative ranges since the document does not report a significance test for the former and does not reproduce the HPQ scale definition for the latter.

Outputs compute the percentage-point gap between trajectory groups and between symptom-count groups in self-reported economic worsening, plus the two presenteeism scores reported as-is. No dollar amounts are computed or implied anywhere in this simulator.

Limitations: the pooled economic-worsening and presenteeism figures used here were not broken down by sex, age, or other demographic subgroup in the source, even though sex and age were collected in the study; federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally supports this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it. The study's own earlier analysis of the same base cohort found a higher long COVID risk among females than males at 12 months (odds ratio 2.54, 95% CI 1.43-4.53), but no significant sex difference was observed in the long-COVID-vs-not comparison at 36 months - these describe two different follow-up time windows, not a single stable sex effect, and should not be merged. The study lacks a healthy-control comparison group and objective biomarker confirmation of long COVID, so the authors themselves note it is unclear whether reported economic-condition changes reflect long COVID specifically versus general pandemic-era circumstances. Findings are specific to this hospitalized Japanese cohort and should not be pooled with non-hospitalized or non-Japanese population estimates.

A similar pattern appeared between patients with five-or-more versus one-to-four symptoms (about 47% vs 24%), though the document does not report a significance test for that specific comparison. These patterns may help identify which post-COVID patients could benefit from earlier vocational or rehabilitation referral, though the study provides no cost or wage data to size that need financially.
takeaway.policy: In this 515-patient Japanese multicenter cohort of adults hospitalized with COVID-19 (waves 1-3, January 2020-February 2021) followed to 36 months, 25.6% (132/515) met the study's long COVID definition at 3 years. Among symptomatic patients, those with a continuous symptom trajectory reported substantially higher rates of self-reported economic worsening (43.6%) than those who recovered (14.9%), a roughly 29-percentage-point gap found statistically significant (p<0.001); a similar, non-significance-tested gap (about 23 percentage points) was observed between patients with five-or-more versus one-to-four symptoms. No direct medical costs, non-medical costs, or monetized productivity losses are reported anywhere in this study - only unitless WHO HPQ presenteeism/absenteeism scores and categorical self-report items from this one hospitalized Japanese cohort.

patient: If experiencing several ongoing long COVID symptoms together, consider raising with a clinician whether exploring work-accommodation or rehabilitation support earlier might be worthwhile, since the study linked having multiple ongoing symptoms with worse self-rated work performance.

When comparing personal experience to this study, keep in mind it followed hospitalized adults in Japan for three years using questionnaires, not a direct measure of costs, and it reported group patterns, not a prediction for any one person.

If a 'presenteeism' or 'absenteeism' score comes up in care discussions, ask what it means in plain terms - it is a self-rated measure of how much symptoms got in the way of work performance, not a diagnosis or a cost figure.
care: Consider whether the 3-month symptom-cluster classification, especially a 'multiple symptoms' pattern, could be worth checking against local follow-up protocols as an early flag for patients who may benefit from earlier occupational-health or rehabilitation referral.

Review whether longer-term follow-up scheduling distinguishes between continuous, relapsing, and recovered symptom trajectories, since these groups diverged sharply in self-reported productivity and economic outcomes in this cohort.

Note that the absenteeism-score comparison between long-COVID and non-long-COVID patients did not reach statistical significance (p=0.94) in this cohort, unlike the presenteeism-score comparison (p=0.003) - avoid treating these two work-impact measures as equally well-supported when designing outreach criteria.

Consider adding a routine self-reported economic-condition follow-up item for long COVID patients, mirroring this study's approach, since no monetized cost data exists in this document to substitute for it.
policy: Treat the trajectory-group and symptom-count patterns as a qualitative, non-monetized signal of which post-COVID patient profiles may warrant longer-term disability or return-to-work policy attention, recognizing this document provides no cost basis for sizing that need.

Consider this study's self-reported economic-worsening percentages (continuous vs recovered groups) as one input worth weighing in disability/accommodation policy discussions, understanding they are subjective single-item self-reports from a hospitalized Japanese cohort, not validated income-loss measures.

Avoid pooling this cohort's 36-month prevalence (25.6%) or productivity-score findings with non-hospitalized or non-Japanese Long COVID surveillance estimates, since they use different populations, case definitions, and settings.

If pursuing cost-effectiveness or burden estimates for long COVID policy, note that this document supplies no dollar or yen figure and would require an external wage/cost model plus a separate monetization methodology not provided here.
